lines.text: Life is marked by significant events that shape who we are. It begins with birth — the arrival of a new life into the world. Early milestones include a christening or naming ceremony, first steps, and starting school. Graduation from school or university marks the transition into professional life. Career milestones follow: landing a first job, earning a promotion, or starting a business. Personal milestones are equally important. Falling in love, getting engaged, and having a wedding are celebrated across cultures. The birth of a child transforms a couple into parents. Buying a first home represents financial independence. Moving to a new city or emigrating to another country can be life-changing. Not all life events are joyful. Losing a job, going through a divorce, experiencing an illness, or suffering bereavement — the death of a loved one — are painful but universal experiences. A funeral brings family together to mourn and remember. Retirement marks the end of a working career and the beginning of a new chapter. Anniversary celebrations — whether of a wedding, a career, or a national event — remind us how far we've come. Each life event, joyful or difficult, contributes to our personal story.

lines.text: When someone dies, English speakers say 'I'm sorry for your loss', 'My condolences', or 'My deepest sympathies'. At funerals, 'Rest in peace' (R.I.P.) is common. Sending a sympathy card is customary in English-speaking cultures.

lines.text: English weddings involve specific vocabulary: the 'ceremony' (official part), the 'reception' (celebration), the 'best man' and 'maid of honour' (key attendants), the 'vows' (promises), the 'aisle' (walkway), and the 'honeymoon' (holiday after the wedding).

lines.text: Certain birthdays carry special significance: 1st (first year), 16th ('sweet sixteen' in USA), 18th (legal adulthood in UK/Australia), 21st (traditional adulthood in USA), 30th, 40th, 50th, and 100th (centenary — often with a royal greeting in the UK).

lines.text: In English-speaking countries, retirement typically occurs between 60-67. A 'retirement party' is customary at work. Retirees often receive a pension. Phrases like 'put your feet up' and 'enjoy your golden years' are common retirement wishes.

lines.text: English-speaking universities hold formal 'commencement' or 'graduation' ceremonies. Graduates wear a 'cap and gown' (academic dress), receive a 'diploma' or 'degree', and toss their caps in the air. Families attend and celebrate with gifts and meals.
